messages.content: Our clinic's brochure says the treatment has an 80% success rate. The trial enrolled 240 patients, 210 finished the treatment, and 168 were cured. Is 80% the honest number to print?
Eighty percent is one honest answer to a question nobody asked carefully. A rate is a numerator over a denominator, and here three denominators are defensible. First, everyone enrolled:
70%. Now only the patients who actually completed the treatment:
That is your brochure's 80%. There is a third cut: of the 210 completers, 190 followed the protocol exactly, and 160 of those were cured:

84.2%. All three numbers are true; they answer different questions. The 70% figure (called intent-to-treat) answers: if a patient like those enrolled starts this treatment, how likely is a cure, counting dropouts as failures? The 84.2% (per-protocol) answers: if a patient finishes and follows it exactly, how well does the drug itself work? The 80% in the middle is the one with no clean question attached. Print 70% in the brochure, because a new patient cannot know in advance whether they will be a completer, and keep 84.2% for the clinicians. A success rate quoted without its denominator is not a statistic, it is a slogan.
The county health report says our town had 36 cases of a rare disease last year. The town has 48,000 people. How do I express that as a rate people can compare with other towns?
Raw counts cannot be compared between towns of different sizes, so divide by population and scale to a standard base. Per 100,000 residents, the standard for rare events:
75 cases per 100,000 people. The same fact on other bases: per 1,000 it is
and as a plain percentage it is

0.075%. All three are the identical rate wearing different clothes: 75 per 100,000 = 0.75 per 1,000 = 0.075%. The scaling choice is about the audience's intuition. Percentages work when the rate is a few percent or more; below that, decimals like 0.075% read as zero and people stop thinking. Per-100,000 turns a rare event into a whole number a reader can hold onto, which is why disease statistics use it. What you must never do is compare one town's count with another town's rate, or two rates on different bases, without converting first.
Our warehouse had 14 recordable injuries last year. We have 380 workers and they logged 412,000 hours total. What is our injury rate?

Per worker is the tempting denominator, but workers are not the exposure: hours are. Someone on site 10 hours a week and someone on 50 do not carry the same risk. The safety industry standard is incidents per 100,000 hours worked:
3.4 injuries per 100,000 hours. Compare the per-worker version:

3.7% of workers were injured, which sounds alarming but mixes full-timers and part-timers into one pool. There is a third common form, per 100 full-time-equivalent years (one FTE-year is 2,000 hours, so your crew is 206 FTE):

6.8 per 100 FTE-years. Same 14 injuries, three rates, each correct for its audience: hours for comparing sites with different shift patterns, FTE for benchmarking against industry tables, per-worker only for a rough internal feel. When someone hands you an injury rate, the first question is always: per what?

A news site reported our city's asthma hospitalization rate as 11.2 per 100,000. But they divided the 212 hospitalizations of city residents by the whole metro area population of 1.9 million. The city itself has 640,000 people. How wrong is the story?
The numerator and denominator describe two different populations, so the rate is simply broken. Their version:
11.2 per 100,000. With the denominator that matches the numerator, city residents over city population:
33.1 per 100,000. The correction factor is the population ratio itself:

The published rate understates the city's true rate by a factor of 2.97, nearly threefold. This is the most common way rates go wrong in print: the numerator is easy to get exactly (hospital records know who was admitted) while the denominator is grabbed from whatever population figure is handy. The discipline is to ask, for every rate, whether the people in the numerator could only have come from the people in the denominator. If the denominator includes people who could never appear in the numerator, the rate is diluted and wrong.
Our delivery fleet drove 2,300,000 miles last year across 46 vans and had 9 crashes. The insurer wants a crash rate. What do I give them?
Insurers rate fleets per mile driven, because miles are the exposure. Per million miles:
3.91 crashes per million miles. On a per-100,000-mile base, the same rate is
0.39. There is also a per-vehicle version, useful for your own planning rather than the insurer's:

19.6 crashes per 100 van-years, or about one crash for every five vans each year. Give the insurer the per-million-mile figure, 3.91, because it stays meaningful if you add vans or change routes, while the per-van figure silently assumes every van drives the same distance. If two of your vans are low-mileage city runners and the rest are highway haulers, even the per-mile rate hides a split worth checking separately.
We run a subscription app. Last year we had 46 service incidents. Our user count grew during the year and averaged 8,400 users. How do I state an incident rate that is fair to a growing product?

Incidents per month would punish you for growing: more users means more chances for something to break. The exposure unit for a subscription product is the user-month, one user subscribed for one month. Your total exposure:
100,800 user-months. The rate:
0.456 incidents per 1,000 user-months. Contrast the naive monthly average:

3.83 incidents a month tells a reader nothing about reliability, because a month with 6,000 users and a month with 10,800 users are not the same amount of exposure. If next year incidents rise to 55 but users average 12,000, the monthly count looks worse while the user-month rate actually improves to 0.382. Rates with an exposure denominator are how growing systems report honestly instead of apologizing for their own growth.
Our shop's site had 96,000 sessions and 71,000 unique visitors last month, with 2,850 orders. Marketing says conversion is about 4%, the analytics tool says about 3%. Who is right?
Both, because they are dividing by different things and calling both conversion. Per session:
2.97%, the analytics tool's number. Per unique visitor:

4.01%, marketing's number. Neither is an error; they are answers to different questions. Per-session conversion measures how well a visit converts, and it is the right rate for judging a landing page or a checkout flow, since one determined buyer may take three sessions to order. Per-visitor conversion measures how many of the people you reached became buyers, the right rate for judging an ad campaign. The fix is not to pick a winner but to name the denominator every time the number is spoken: conversion per session, 2.97%; conversion per visitor, 4.01%. A rate whose denominator has to be guessed will be guessed in whoever's favor is speaking.
Our town of 62,500 people recorded 715 births and 540 deaths last year. The council wants the birth rate and death rate in the usual form.
Vital statistics are conventionally quoted per 1,000 population per year. Births:
11.44 births per 1,000 people. Deaths:
8.64 per 1,000. The difference is the rate of natural increase:

2.8 per 1,000, meaning the town grows by about 0.28% a year from births and deaths alone, before migration. Two cautions when the council compares these with other towns. First, crude rates like these are hostage to age structure: a retirement town will show a high death rate even with excellent health care, because its denominator is old. Second, with counts in the hundreds, a single unusual month can move the second decimal, so quote one decimal at most: 11.4 and 8.6 per 1,000.
Our hospital discharged 1,240 patients and 186 were readmitted within 30 days, so I reported a 15% readmission rate. Our quality officer says that is not the right denominator. Why not?
Your arithmetic is right and the denominator is still wrong for the question. The crude rate:

15.0%. But 74 of those 1,240 patients died during their stay. A patient who died cannot be readmitted, so they were never at risk of entering your numerator, and keeping them in the denominator dilutes the rate. Excluding them:
16.0% (186 of 1,166). There is a second refinement: 12 of the 186 readmissions were planned procedures booked before discharge, which are not failures of care. Unplanned readmissions only:

14.9%. So one dataset yields 15.0%, 16.0%, and 14.9%, and the quality officer's point is that each serves a different purpose: the crude rate for capacity planning, the at-risk rate for comparing hospitals, the unplanned rate for judging discharge quality. The rule underneath all of it: everyone in the denominator must be capable of appearing in the numerator.

In our study, 214 volunteers were followed for different lengths of time, totaling 1,930 person-years of observation, and we saw 58 new cases of the condition. A colleague reported this as 27% of participants. Is that a fair summary?
It is a true fraction and a misleading rate. The headcount version:
27.1% of participants developed the condition. But participants were not observed equally: average follow-up was

9.02 years, with some followed for 2 years and some for 15. A person watched for 15 years has far more opportunity to become a case than one watched for 2, so the headcount rate cannot be compared with any other study. The person-time rate fixes this:

30.05 cases per 1,000 person-years. That number is portable: another study with different follow-up lengths can be set beside it directly. Whenever follow-up varies, or people enter and leave a group over time, the denominator belongs in units of people multiplied by time, not people alone. Your colleague's 27% is not wrong as a description of this cohort; it is useless as a rate.
My investment went up 50% last year and down 50% this year, so I figure I am back where I started. I put in $80,000. Am I?
You are not, and the reason is that the two 50%s act on different bases. Up 50% on $80,000:
$120,000. Down 50% now takes half of the larger amount:
$60,000. Your overall change:

You are down 25%, not flat. Percentage changes do not cancel because each one is computed on whatever the value happens to be at that moment. A gain inflates the base that the next loss feeds on, and a loss shrinks the base the next gain can rebuild from. The symmetric-sounding pair +50% and -50% always nets to -25%, whatever the starting amount. To undo a 50% loss you do not need a 50% gain; you need a 100% gain, because you are rebuilding from half the money.
The news says the central bank raised rates by 1%, but my brother says rates went from 4% to 5%, which is a 25% increase. One of them must be wrong.
Neither is wrong; they are using two different units that share the word percent. The move from 4% to 5% is one percentage point:
A percentage point is the plain arithmetic difference between two percentages. As a relative change, measured against the starting rate:

25%. Both statements describe the same event. The confusion is expensive: if your savings account advertises that its rate rose 25%, you might expect 4% to become 29%, when it became 5%. Watch the same trap in softer form: a party's support rising from 62% to 68% is up 6 points, but up only

9.7% in relative terms. Rule of thumb: when the thing changing is itself a percentage, demand to know whether the change is quoted in points or in percent. Headlines pick whichever sounds bigger; honest reports give the two levels and let you compute both.

A headline brags that a corner bakery grew its Saturday crowd by 125% while the big grocery chain only managed 10% growth. The bakery went from 40 to 90 Saturday customers. The chain went from 40,000 to 44,000. Who actually grew more?
Check the percentages first. The bakery:
125%, as advertised. The chain:
10%. Now the absolute gains the headline declined to mention. The bakery added 90 - 40 = 50 customers. The chain added

4,000 customers, eighty times the bakery's gain. This is the base effect: a percentage change is a gain divided by a starting point, so a tiny base manufactures spectacular percentages out of trivial changes. Neither number is false, but they answer different questions. The percentage tells you the bakery's momentum relative to its size; the absolute tells you where the customers actually went. Any growth claim on a small base should be read with the base attached, and any comparison between a small base and a large one should show both the percent and the count.
A jacket was $80, the store raised it 25%, and now it is on sale. How much does the sale need to cut to get back to $80? My friend says 25% off. I am not so sure.
Your friend is wrong, and your doubt is well placed. The raised price:
$100. A 25% cut from $100 would leave $75, too much off. The cut that lands exactly on $80:
20% off. The general rule: to undo a rise of r percent, divide by (1 + r/100); the equivalent cut is always smaller than the rise. Undoing a 50% rise takes a cut of

33.3%, and undoing a 100% rise takes 50% off. The asymmetry is the same one that makes a 50% loss require a 100% gain to repair: percentages are always computed on the current value, and after the first move the current value is no longer the one you started with. When a store advertises a rise followed by an equal-looking discount, the till keeps the difference.
Our unit sales changed by +10% in January, -5% in February, and +8% in March. I added them up and told my boss we grew 13% this quarter. She says that is not how it works.
Your boss is right: percentage changes chain by multiplying, not by adding. Start with a round 500 units in December and apply each month in turn. January:
550. February's -5% acts on 550, not on 500:
522.5. March's +8% acts on that:
564.3 units. The quarter's true growth:

12.86%, not 13%. The gap looks small here, but it grows with the size and number of the changes, and it can flip signs: +40% then -30% sums to +10% but multiplies to 1.4 x 0.7 = 0.98, an actual loss of 2%. Adding percentages treats every change as if it acted on the original base; multiplying respects the fact that each change acts on the result of the last. For any sequence of changes, multiply the (1 + rate) factors and subtract 1 at the end.
My portfolio dropped from $200,000 to $120,000. My advisor says I need a 40% gain to get back to even, since I lost 40%. That sounds off to me.
It is off, in the direction that hurts. You lost
40% of the original value. But the recovery gain is computed on what you have now, $120,000, and you need to rebuild $80,000:
You need a 66.7% gain, not 40%. Check: $120,000 grown by 40% is only

$168,000, still $32,000 short. The general pattern is worth memorizing: a loss of L percent needs a gain of L/(100-L) percent to repair it. Lose 10%, need 11.1%. Lose 25%, need 33.3%. Lose 50%, need 100%. Lose 75%, need 300%. This is why deep drawdowns are so destructive and why the advisor's version is dangerous: it understates the climb by using the pre-loss base. Whenever someone quotes you a recovery target, ask which base it is computed on.
A coat is $120. The store takes 30% off, and at the register there is an extra 20% off the sale price. The sign says 50% off total if you add them. What do I actually pay?
The sign is doing the adding-percentages trick. First discount:
$84. The extra 20% comes off the $84, not the $120:
$67.20. Your true total discount:

44% off, not 50%. Each successive discount acts on a smaller base, so stacked percentages always deliver less than their sum: 30% then 20% multiplies to 0.7 x 0.8 = 0.56, meaning you pay 56% of the original. Retailers love the additive framing because 30 + 20 sounds like 50. The same mathematics runs in your favor with stacked gains, by the way: two successive 20% rises compound to 44%, more than their sum, because the second rise acts on the enlarged base.
Our startup's profit went from -$50,000 last year to +$50,000 this year. My spreadsheet formula says the percentage change is -200%, which is obviously nonsense. What is going on?
Your formula is doing exactly what it was told, and the concept itself has broken. The standard formula, (new - old) / old:
-200%, claiming a catastrophic decline in a year when profit improved by $100,000. The sign of the base poisons everything. Watch it fail the other way: an improvement from -$50,000 to -$10,000 gives

-80%, again reporting a loss year as a decline. Percentage change is only meaningful when the base is positive, because the formula divides by the base and a negative base flips the sign of every improvement. When a series crosses zero, or starts negative, the honest report is the absolute change: profit improved by $100,000, swinging from a $50,000 loss to a $50,000 profit. Analysts write n/m (not meaningful) in the percent column for exactly this situation. It is not a spreadsheet bug to fix; it is a question the percentage cannot answer.
I got a 3% raise last year and a 4% raise this year on my $60,000 salary. Payroll says my total raise over the two years is 7.12%, but 3 + 4 is 7. Are they overpaying me?
Payroll is right, and sadly nobody is overpaying you; the second raise acted on your already-raised salary. After year one:
$61,800. The 4% raise applies to that:
$64,272. Total change over the two years:

7.12%. The extra 0.12% is the raise on the raise: 4% of the first year's $1,800 increase is $72, which is exactly the gap between $64,272 and the $64,200 you would get from a flat 7%. Successive percentage changes always multiply: 1.03 x 1.04 = 1.0712. The effect is small for small raises over short spans, which is why the additive shortcut survives in casual speech, but over a career of annual raises it is the difference between a rough guess and your actual salary.
Our town's population fell 20% during the mill closure years, from 12,500. Since the new plant opened it has grown 20%. The mayor says the town is back to full strength. Is it?
Run the two moves in order. The decline:
10,000 people. The 20% growth acts on 10,000, not on the original 12,500:
12,000 people. The town is still short

4% of its former population, 500 people. The mayor's error is treating +20% and -20% as inverse operations. They are not: the fall was measured on the larger base and the recovery on the smaller one, so equal percentages produce unequal headcounts, 2,500 lost against 2,000 regained. To fully recover from a 20% fall the town would need 25% growth on its reduced base. This asymmetry is why percent declines in population, membership, or revenue should always be reported alongside the counts: the percentages alone can make a town that is still 500 people short sound whole.
If I put $10,000 in an account paying 8% a year for 10 years, how much more does compound interest give me than simple interest?
Simple interest pays 8% of the original $10,000 every year and never a cent on the interest itself. Total interest:
$8,000, for a final balance of $18,000. Compound interest pays each year's 8% on everything accumulated so far:
$21,589.25. The compounding premium:

$3,589.25 extra, from interest earning interest. Notice the premium is not a fixed slice: after one year the two accounts are identical, and the gap only widens as the interest pile itself starts earning. Over 10 years at 8% the premium is about 20% of the simple-interest outcome; over 30 years the compound balance would be $100,626.57 against $34,000 simple, nearly triple. Time is the ingredient compounding feeds on, which is why the same rate is a modest perk in a savings account and the whole story in a retirement account.
Our revenue grew from $2.4 million to $3.9 million over five years. What was our average annual growth rate? I do not want to just divide 62.5% by 5.

Good instinct: dividing the total by 5 gives 12.5%, which overstates it, because growth compounds. The compound annual growth rate, CAGR, asks what single yearly rate, applied five times, carries 2.4 to 3.9:
10.2% per year. Verify by compounding it forward:
$3.90 million, back where you ended. The naive 12.5% would have predicted

$4.32 million, more than you actually made. CAGR uses only the two endpoints and the elapsed time, which makes it the right tool for comparing growth across companies or periods of different lengths. Its weakness is the same as its convenience: it says nothing about the path. Two firms with identical CAGRs may have grown smoothly or lurched; the rate cannot tell you, and we will see in a moment why that matters.
A fund reports a smooth 4.88% CAGR over four years. Its actual yearly values were 100, 160, 90, 150, 121. How can the CAGR be so calm when the years were that wild?
Compute the year-by-year changes. Year one:
+60%. Year two:
-43.75%. Year three:
+66.67%. Year four:
-19.33%. Now the CAGR from endpoints alone:

4.88%, exactly as reported. CAGR is a function of the first value, the last value, and the count of years; the three middle values could be anything at all and the rate would not move. An investor who lived through a 43.75% drawdown experienced a completely different investment from the smooth 4.88% the brochure implies. This is the smoothness lie: CAGR is an honest answer to 'what constant rate connects the endpoints?' and a dishonest impression of 'what was it like to hold this?' Always ask for the yearly path, or at least the worst year, beside any CAGR.
People quote the rule of 72 for doubling times: at 6% money doubles in 12 years. How accurate is that rule, and where does it break?
Test it by compounding. At 6%, twelve years of growth:

1.06^12 = 2.012, slightly more than double, so the true doubling time is a touch under 12 years (11.90 exactly). The rule of 72 says 72/6 = 12: excellent. Now push the rate up. At 24% the rule promises a double in 3 years:
1.907, not yet doubled; the true time is about 3.22 years. At 36% the rule says 2 years:

1.850, well short; the truth is about 2.25 years. The pattern: the rule of 72 is a linearization of the logarithm, calibrated to be nearly exact near 8%, and it drifts low as rates climb, understating doubling time by roughly 11% at 36%. For everyday rates between about 2% and 15% it is a fine mental tool. For the returns promised by speculative schemes, which is exactly where people reach for it, it flatters the pitch. When the rate is high, do the compounding, not the rule.
Our subscriber base is shrinking 20% a year from 50,000. A board member said if this keeps up we lose 10,000 a year and are gone in five years. Is that the right picture?
The rate is right and the picture is wrong, because a constant percentage decline takes a shrinking absolute bite each year. Year one ends at
40,000, a loss of 10,000. Year two loses 20% of 40,000, which is 8,000, ending at 32,000. Year three:
25,600, a loss of 6,400 that year. After five years you would hold

16,384 subscribers, not zero. A constant percentage decline is exponential decay: it halves roughly every 3.1 years here and never quite reaches zero. The board member's straight-line picture (10,000 a year, gone in five) describes a constant absolute decline, a different and worse disease. Neither picture is comforting, but they demand different responses: a percentage bleed can be survived while you fix the cause, and its losses shrink as the base shrinks. Confusing the two leads boards to panic at the wrong speed.
Our startup has 8% market share growing 30% a year. An investor deck projects that rate forward ten years. Should I be embarrassed by that slide?
Run the projection and watch where it lands. After five years:
29.7% share, plausible enough. After nine years:
84.8%. After ten:

110.3% of the market, which is impossible: a share is a part of a whole and cannot pass 100%. The growth rate must slow long before then, because the remaining customers get harder to win and competitors respond. This is the ceiling problem with extrapolating any percentage growth in a bounded quantity: market share, adoption rates, capacity utilization, and conversion rates all live under a cap, and exponential curves do not respect caps. The honest slide shows the growth rate bending down, often an S-curve, with the assumptions stated. If a projection has a share passing about half the market at an undiminished rate, the model is not optimistic; it is broken.
A loan advertises 12% interest compounded monthly. A friend says that is really the same as 12% a year. Is it?
Not quite. Compounded monthly means 1% is charged each month, and each month's interest itself starts earning interest. The effective annual rate:
12.68%, not 12%. On $10,000 that is $1,268 of interest in a year instead of $1,200. Compounding quarterly instead gives

12.55%. The pattern: the quoted 12% is a nominal rate, a label; the effective rate depends on how often interest is folded into the base. More frequent compounding always raises the effective rate at the same nominal number. This is why regulations require lenders and banks to disclose an effective annual figure (APR/APY): it is the only version of the rate that can be compared across products with different compounding schedules. Whenever two rates are compared, first make sure both are effective over the same period.
A stock picker brags that his two-year returns averaged +25% a year: up 100% the first year, down 50% the second. His investors seem unimpressed. What are they seeing?
Follow $100 through his two years. Up 100%:

$100. The investor ends exactly where they started, a 0% total return. The brag uses the arithmetic mean of the two yearly rates, (100 + (-50))/2 = +25%, which is the wrong average for chained changes because the years do not act on the same base. The correct average is the geometric mean of the growth factors:

0% per year, matching reality. Arithmetic means are for quantities that add; growth factors multiply, so they must be averaged by multiplying (and taking the root). Any 'average return' quoted for a multi-year investment should be the geometric one, which is exactly what CAGR is. If someone averages percentage returns with ordinary addition, their average will always flatter a volatile record, because volatility itself drags the geometric mean below the arithmetic one.
A bacteria culture starts with 500 cells and doubles every 20 minutes. How many cells after 3 hours, and why does my calculator friend say the answer is not 500 plus nine small additions?
Three hours is 180 minutes, which is nine doubling periods. Doubling means multiplying by 2 each period, so nine periods multiply by 2^9:
512. The final count:
256,000 cells. After just two hours (six doublings) it was already

32,000. Your friend is pointing at the difference between additive and multiplicative growth: each new cell also divides, so the growth itself grows. The last doubling alone adds 128,000 cells, more than the first eight doublings combined added. This is why exponential processes feel deceptively calm early and overwhelming late, and why the right question about any doubling process is never 'how much did it grow?' but 'how many doublings fit in the time available?'
App A grew from 12,000 to 30,000 users in three years. App B grew from 40,000 to 70,000 in the same three years. A founder friend says A grew faster. My co-founder says B grew more. Settle it.
Both are right, about different quantities. Growth rate first, using CAGR. App A multiplied by 2.5 over three years:
35.7% per year. App B multiplied by 1.75:
20.5% per year. So A grew faster in rate. In absolute terms A added
18,000 users, while B added

30,000 users. Rate and amount are different measurements and they routinely crown different winners, because a rate divides by the starting base and B started more than three times larger. Which one matters depends on the decision: momentum and efficiency arguments want the rate; revenue, server load, and support tickets arrive in absolute counts. The mistake is not picking either one; it is letting a single word, 'grew', smuggle the choice past you. Ask: faster, or more?
A class has 14 boys and 21 girls. A report says the ratio of boys to girls is 2:3 and also that boys are 40% of the class. How can both be true?

Because a ratio and a share divide by different things. The ratio compares part to part, boys against girls: 14:21, and dividing both sides by 7 gives 2:3. The share compares part to whole. The whole class:
35 students. Boys as a share:
40%. And girls:

60%. The trap is converting carelessly between the two forms: a 2:3 ratio does not mean boys are 2/3 of anything; it means for every 2 boys there are 3 girls, so boys are 2 of every 5 students. To go from a ratio a:b to a share, divide a by (a + b). Reports exploit the ambiguity when they say a group 'outnumbers another 2 to 1' (a ratio, meaning 66.7% of the pair) in a context where readers hear a share of some larger whole. Always ask: is the second number the other part, or the total?
A bookmaker offers odds of 5:2 on a horse, and a weather app says there is a 75% chance of rain. How do odds and probability convert? They feel like different languages.

They are two notations for the same belief. Probability is favorable outcomes over all outcomes; odds are favorable against unfavorable. Start with the rain: a 75% probability means 75 favorable to 25 unfavorable out of 100, which reduces to odds of 3:1. As a calculation, odds = p/(1-p):
3, hence 3 to 1. Now the horse at 5:2. Converting odds a:b back to probability, divide the favorable by the total of both:
A 71.4% implied probability. And odds of 1:4 against, a long shot, convert to

20%. The conversion rule is symmetric: probability to odds, divide by the complement; odds to probability, divide by the sum. Confusion between them is not harmless: 'the odds are 3 to 1' and 'a 3 in 1 chance' get used interchangeably in speech, but the first means 75% and the second is gibberish that usually intends 33%. When a number really matters, force it into probability, where the denominator is always the whole.

My lender cares about my debt-to-income ratio. My monthly debt payments are $1,450 and my gross monthly income is $5,800. Where do I stand, and what is the most payment I could carry at their 36% limit?
Debt-to-income is total monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income:
25%. You are under the 36% ceiling. The maximum payment at that ceiling on your income:
$2,088 a month, so you have $638 of headroom. One warning about flipped ratios: the same figures can be stated as income-to-debt,

4.0, meaning your income is four times your payments. Both ratios are correct, but they run in opposite directions: for debt-to-income, smaller is safer; for income-to-debt, bigger is safer. A flipped ratio in a report can make an improving situation look like a worsening one if the reader assumes the usual direction. Whenever a ratio is quoted, state it as a sentence: 'payments are 25% of income' cannot be misread; 'the ratio is 0.25' can.
A pancake recipe serves 4 and uses 300 g of flour, 400 mL of milk, and 3 eggs. I need to serve 7 people. How do I scale it without wrecking the batter?
Scaling a recipe is multiplying every ingredient by the same ratio, 7 servings over 4:
A factor of 1.75. Flour:
525 g. Milk:
700 mL. Eggs:

5.25 eggs, the one ingredient that does not come in fractions. In practice you would use 5 whole eggs plus one yolk, accepting a tiny deviation, because eggs are discrete units while flour and milk are continuous. That is the general lesson of proportional scaling: the mathematics multiplies everything by one factor, but the physical world quantizes some ingredients. Scale the continuous ones exactly, round the discrete ones thoughtfully, and never scale the pan size or cooking time by the same factor; a double batch in a bigger pan cooks on a different clock. Ratios preserve flavor; they do not preserve physics.
I mix 200 mL of a 10% salt solution with 300 mL of a 25% salt solution. What is the concentration of the result? My lab partner averaged 10 and 25 and said 17.5%.
Your partner averaged the percentages without weighting them by volume. Track the salt itself. From the first solution:
20 mL of salt (in solution terms). From the second:
75. Total salt 95 in a total volume of 500 mL:

19%, not 17.5%. The correct average is weighted by the volumes: the 25% solution contributes more liquid, so it pulls the result closer to 25. The plain average 17.5% would only be right for equal volumes. This is the mixture rule, and it is the same weighted-average machinery behind blended prices, combined test scores from unequal groups, and average speeds over unequal times. Whenever you average rates or percentages, ask what each one should be weighted by; the weights are usually the denominators the percentages were hiding.
A motor spins a 12-tooth gear at 960 rpm, driving a 48-tooth gear. How fast does the big gear turn, and what do I get in exchange for the lost speed?
Meshed gears trade speed for torque in proportion to their teeth. The gear ratio is
4 to 1: the small gear turns four times for every turn of the large one. Output speed:

240 rpm. In exchange, ignoring friction losses, the output torque is multiplied by the same factor of 4, because the power (speed times torque) is roughly conserved: quarter the speed, quadruple the turning force. This is the same bargain a bicycle's gears offer: the low gear that gets you up a hill spins your legs fast and the wheel slowly but forcefully. One caution for real machines: the ratio sets the ideal trade, and friction takes its fee from both sides, so a real gearbox delivers slightly less torque than the teeth promise. But the speed ratio itself is exact; teeth cannot slip, which is why gears, unlike belts, are used where timing matters.
A 1,750 rpm motor has a pulley 10 cm across, belt-driving a pulley 25 cm across on a saw. How fast does the saw pulley turn?
A belt moves at one speed along its whole length, so each pulley's rim speed must match it, which means rotation speed scales inversely with diameter. The ratio:
0.4. The driven pulley turns at

700 rpm. The larger pulley turns slower in exact proportion to how much bigger it is, and gains torque in the same proportion, here 2.5 times. Compare this with the gear case: pulleys and gears obey the same inverse-ratio law, diameter or teeth standing in for size. The difference is that a belt can slip under overload, which quietly breaks the ratio, while gear teeth cannot. When a belt-driven machine's output speed is measured below the ratio's prediction, the ratio is not wrong; the belt is telling you it is slipping, which is diagnostic information a gear would never give you, it would just jam or break.
On a 1:50,000 map, the distance between two villages measures 7.3 cm. How far apart are they really, and how do I use this scale quickly in the field?
A scale of 1:50,000 means one unit on the map represents 50,000 of the same unit on the ground. Your measured distance:
365,000 cm. Convert to kilometers by dividing by 100,000:

3.65 km. The field shortcut: on this scale 1 cm is 500 m, and 2 cm is exactly 1 km, so you can pace off distances in 2 cm blocks. Two disciplines matter with map scales. First, the scale is a ratio, so it is unit-free: it works in centimeters, inches, or thumb-widths as long as both sides use the same unit. Second, it measures straight-line distance; the walking route between those villages will be longer, sometimes much longer in hill country. A ratio like 1:50,000 is a promise about the map's geometry, not about the journey.
Everyone says 1920x1080 is a 16:9 screen. My laptop is 1366x768 and also claims to be 16:9. Is one of them lying?
Check both divisions. The desktop standard:
1.7778, and 16/9 is exactly 1.7778, so 1920x1080 is a true 16:9. The laptop:
1.7786, close but not equal. A true 16:9 panel at 768 rows would need

1,365.33 columns, and since pixels are indivisible, the manufacturer rounded to 1366. Your laptop's aspect ratio is 683:384, marketed as 16:9. The difference is a quarter of one percent, invisible in practice, but it illustrates how ratios behave in the physical world: a ratio is an exact relationship between integers, and real products approximate it. The practical consequence is tiny: video scaled to the panel is stretched by less than the width of a single pixel column. When a ratio really matters, in machining or optics, you verify it by division, not by the label.
A cleaning concentrate says dilute 1:9. I need 2.5 liters of working solution. How much concentrate and how much water? A colleague says just take a ninth of 2.5 liters as concentrate.
Your colleague has fallen for the classic ratio ambiguity. A dilution of 1:9 means 1 part concentrate plus 9 parts water, 10 parts in total. So the concentrate is one tenth of the final volume:
250 mL of concentrate, and 2,250 mL of water. Your colleague's method, a ninth of the total:

277.8 mL, about 11% too much concentrate. The error comes from reading 1:9 as the fraction 1/9. A ratio a:b describes parts of a mixture whose whole is a + b parts; the fraction of the first component is a/(a + b). Here that is 1/10, not 1/9. The same confusion appears with odds (5:2 means a probability of 5/7, not 5/2 of anything) and with part-to-part ratios generally. Whenever a ratio is handed to you, ask: parts of what whole? Then divide by the sum of the parts.
I drove 120 km at 60 km/h, then another 120 km at 40 km/h through roadworks. My average speed for the trip: my son says 50 km/h, the average of 60 and 40. Is he right?
He would be right if you had spent equal time at each speed, but you spent equal distance, and that changes everything. Average speed is total distance over total time, so find the times. First leg:
2 hours. Second leg:
3 hours. Total: 240 km in 5 hours:

48 km/h, not 50. The slow leg dominates because you spent three hours in it and only two in the fast leg; the average is time-weighted, and equal distances hand more time to the slower speed. This is the harmonic mean in disguise, and it is why 'average speed' questions are traps: averaging the speeds themselves (the arithmetic mean) is only correct when the times at each speed are equal. For equal distances the true average always falls below the simple average of the speeds, and the gap widens as the speeds diverge. A 100 km/h leg and a 20 km/h leg over equal distances average 33.3 km/h, nowhere near 60.
A tank holds 450 liters. A pump fills it at 15 liters a minute while a drain leaks 6 liters a minute. The tank currently has 90 liters in it. How long until it is full?
Rates that oppose each other combine by subtraction. The net fill rate is 15 - 6 = 9 liters a minute. The volume still needed:
360 liters. Time at the net rate:
40 minutes. From empty it would take 360's bigger sibling,

50 minutes. Two lessons hide in this simple problem. First, always combine simultaneous rates before dividing; computing a fill time from the pump alone (30 minutes) and then adjusting for the leak invites error. Second, notice what happens as the leak approaches the fill rate: at a 14-liter leak the net is 1 liter a minute and the fill takes 7.5 hours; at 15 the tank never fills at all. Net-rate problems have a cliff at zero that the raw numbers disguise, which is why 'we are filling faster than we are draining, barely' deserves more alarm than it usually gets.
Ana can paint a room in 6 hours, Ben can paint the same room in 3 hours. Working together, my brother says they will take 4.5 hours, the average. Please tell me he is wrong.
He is wrong, and the correct answer is better than his. Do not average the times; add the rates. Ana paints 1/6 of a room per hour, Ben paints 1/3. Combined rate:
0.5 rooms per hour. Time for one room at that rate:

2 hours. Sanity check: in 2 hours Ana paints a third of the room and Ben paints two thirds; together, one room. The average-of-times answer, 4.5 hours, fails an obvious smell test, since it is slower than Ben working alone. Rates add when workers work in parallel; times never do. The same structure governs parallel resistors, combined data pipes, and two pumps filling one tank. Whenever the problem gives you 'time to complete one job', invert each time into a rate, add the rates, and invert back at the end.
I need to download a 4.7 GB file on a 25 Mbps connection before a meeting. My colleague estimated about 3 minutes. I think he forgot something. How long will it really take?

Your colleague divided gigabytes by megabits without converting, the most common unit error in all of computing rates. File sizes are in bytes; connection speeds are in bits. The file in megabits (using 1 GB = 1,000 MB, the networking convention):
37,600 megabits. At 25 megabits per second:
1,504 seconds. In minutes:

About 25.07 minutes, not 3. His estimate was exactly the forgotten factor of 8: without it you get 188 seconds. Even the honest 25 minutes is a floor, since protocol overhead and a connection that rarely sustains its headline rate will stretch it; budget 30. The discipline: in any rate calculation, write the units beside the numbers and cancel them like fractions. If the units do not cancel to the unit you want, the arithmetic is wrong no matter how clean the digits look.
My resting heart rate is 72 beats per minute. A fitness article says my heart beats about 100,000 times a day. That seems like a lot. Is it right?
Multiply it out. Beats per hour:
4,320. Per day:
103,680 beats, so the article's 'about 100,000' is honest rounding. Per year:

37,843,200, roughly 38 million beats a year, and over an 80-year life on the order of 3 billion. Rates become staggering when the time base stretches, which is precisely why per-minute is the natural unit for a heart and per-day would be useless to a doctor. The same arithmetic in reverse is a good sanity tool: if a device claims a million cycles a day, that is about 11.6 cycles a second, every second, which either matches its design or exposes the claim. Whenever a rate surprises you, convert it to the time base you can picture and check it there.
We have two office printers rated at 18 pages per minute each, and a 5,400-page report run to finish. How long on both printers, and how long if one breaks?
Parallel machines add their rates, exactly like the two painters. Combined:
36 pages per minute. The run takes
150 minutes, two and a half hours. With one printer down, the rate halves and the time doubles:

300 minutes, five hours. Notice the asymmetry this creates for planning: losing one of two printers doubles the job time, while losing one of ten would only add about 11%. Redundancy math is rate math. One more real-world adjustment: the 18 ppm rating is the engine speed once running, and first-page-out time, warm-up, and paper refills mean a short job never achieves it. For a 5,400-page run the rating is a fair guide; for a 3-page memo, the rate is nearly meaningless and the fixed delays are the whole story.
My car's consumption is rated 8.4 liters per 100 km. I am driving 640 km and fuel costs $1.62 a liter. What will the fuel cost, roughly?
Consumption per 100 km is a rate with a slightly unusual base. Fuel needed is the rate times the number of 100-km blocks:
53.76 liters. At $1.62 a liter:

$87.09. The per-kilometer form of the same rate is 0.084 liters, which some drivers find easier: every 100 km costs about $13.61. European-style consumption figures (liters per 100 km) run backwards compared with miles per gallon: with L/100 km, a smaller number is better, while with mpg a bigger number is better. That inversion has fooled many a car buyer comparing across systems. To convert, divide 235.2 by the mpg figure to get L/100 km. However it is expressed, the skill is the same: get the rate onto the base of your actual trip before you multiply.
A hospital IV order reads: 500 mL over 4 hours, drip factor 20 drops per mL. The nurse needs the drip rate in drops per minute. Walk me through it.
Two rates chained together. First the flow rate in volume per hour:
125 mL per hour. Convert to drops per hour using the drip factor, then to drops per minute:
41.67 drops per minute. Since a nurse cannot set two thirds of a drop, the practical setting is about 42 drops a minute, or one drop every

1.44 seconds, which is what she will actually count against her watch. Every step here is a unit conversion riding on a rate: hours to minutes, milliliters to drops. This is the class of calculation where a factor-of-60 error is easiest to make and hardest to catch by feel, because 41.67 and 2,500 drops per minute do not look equally plausible until you ask how many seconds sit between drops. In safety-critical rate work, always finish by converting the answer into the interval a human can observe.
A cyclist covers 24 km in 50 minutes. My computer at home says her speed in km/h, but a physics problem wants meters per second. Give me both.
Speed is distance over time with the time in the unit the answer wants. For km/h, express 50 minutes as a fraction of an hour:
28.8 km/h. To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6 (because an hour holds 3,600 seconds and a kilometer holds 1,000 meters):

Exactly 8 m/s. The 3.6 conversion factor is worth memorizing: multiply m/s by 3.6 for km/h, divide km/h by 3.6 for m/s. Sanity anchors help catch direction errors: 10 m/s is 36 km/h, a fast sprint on a bike; 30 m/s is 108 km/h, highway speed. If a conversion gives you a cyclist at 103.7 m/s, you multiplied when you should have divided, and the anchors expose it instantly. Rates with compound units always carry their conversion factors inside them; the units are part of the number.
Streaming video uses about 5 Mbps. If I watch a two-hour film, how much of my 10 GB monthly data cap does it eat?
Data used is rate times time, with a bits-to-bytes conversion at the end. Total bits streamed:
36,000 megabits over the 7,200 seconds. Divide by 8 for bytes:

4,500 MB, which is 4.5 GB: nearly half your 10 GB cap on one film. Two such films leave you 1 GB for everything else. The levers are all in the rate: dropping the stream quality to 2.5 Mbps halves the consumption to 2.25 GB, because data use is strictly proportional to bitrate at fixed time. This is why 'unlimited' home broadband and capped mobile data produce such different viewing habits: the same film costs nothing measurable on one and half a month's allowance on the other. Whenever a rate is quoted per second and your budget is per month, the conversion is where the surprise lives.

A study compared two kidney-stone treatments. Treatment A succeeded in 93% of small-stone cases and 73% of large-stone cases. Treatment B succeeded in 87% and 69%. But overall B beat A, 83% to 78%. That is impossible, surely?
It is possible, and it has a name: Simpson's paradox. Put the actual counts on the table. A on small stones, 81 successes of 87:
93.1%. A on large stones, 192 of 263:
73.0%. B on small stones, 234 of 270:
86.7%. B on large stones, 55 of 80:
68.8%. A wins both subgroups, as you said. Now the pooled rates. A treated 350 patients with 273 successes:
78.0%. B treated 350 with 289:

82.6%. The resolution is in the case mix: A drew the hard cases, 263 of its 350 patients had large stones, while B's list was 270 small-stone patients out of 350. Large stones succeed less often under either treatment, so A's pooled rate is dragged down by its harder workload, not by worse medicine. A pooled rate is a weighted average of subgroup rates, and the weights are the group sizes. Whenever groups are mixed in different proportions, the pooled comparison can reverse the honest subgroup comparison. Compare like with like, subgroup by subgroup, or adjust for the mix.
Two clinics both report a 66.7% success rate. Clinic A treated 3 patients, clinic B treated 300. My manager says the rates are identical so the clinics are equal. Something feels wrong.
The rates are identical as fractions:
and
both 66.7%. What differs is how much the next patient can move the number. One more failure at clinic A:
50%, a collapse of 16.7 points. One more failure at clinic B:

66.4%, a wobble of 0.3 points. A rate is an estimate of an underlying performance, and the denominator is the evidence behind the estimate. Two successes in three tries is consistent with a clinic whose true rate is anywhere from mediocre to excellent; two hundred in three hundred pins it down. This is why a rate should never travel without its counts: '66.7% (2 of 3)' and '66.7% (200 of 300)' are the same number and completely different claims. Rankings built on small denominators are mostly rankings of luck.
A newspaper ranked our three regional hospitals by deaths last year: Hospital B worst with 30 deaths, then A with 12, then C with 8. Patient numbers were A 400, B 3,000, C 90. Is B really the worst?
The newspaper ranked counts, not rates, and the hospitals differ thirtyfold in size. Convert each to a death rate. A:

8.9%. The ranking reverses completely: B, the supposed worst, has the lowest death rate, and C, the supposed best, has the highest by a wide margin. Raw outcome counts measure size as much as quality. This is the league-table fallacy, and it is everywhere: crime by city, accidents by airline, complaints by company, all meaningless until divided by the exposure. Two refinements still matter after the division. C's rate rests on only 90 patients, so it is a fragile estimate; and hospitals taking sicker patients will show worse rates for better care, the case-mix problem. But the first, non-negotiable step is the one the newspaper skipped: no denominator, no ranking.

Town A's death rate is 5.8 per 1,000 and Town B's is 21 per 1,000. A regional paper says B's health services are failing. But both towns have identical age-specific death rates: 2 per 1,000 for under-65s and 40 per 1,000 for over-65s. What is going on?
The towns differ in who lives there, not in how people fare. Town A has 9,000 younger and 1,000 older residents. Its deaths:
18 + 40 = 58 deaths among 10,000 people, the crude rate of 5.8 per 1,000. Town B has 5,000 of each:

10 + 200 = 210 deaths, a crude rate of 21 per 1,000. Every age group dies at exactly the same rate in both towns; B simply has five times the share of older residents, and older residents die at twenty times the younger rate. To compare fairly, apply both towns' age-specific rates to one standard population, say half young and half old:

Both towns standardize to 21 per 1,000: identical. This is age standardization, and it exists because a crude rate is a weighted average whose weights are the population's own age mix. Any comparison of death, disease, or crime rates between places with different demographics needs the adjustment, or it is comparing demography wearing the mask of performance.

An ad says the average fund in a fund family returned 9% a year over the last decade. The family started the decade with 100 funds. Forty of them still exist and averaged +9%. Sixty were closed along the way after averaging -6%. What did the average investor's fund actually do?
The ad averages only the survivors. Weight all 100 funds, the ones you could actually have bought at the start:

0% a year. The advertised 9% and the experienced 0% differ by the entire graveyard. This is survivorship bias in rate form: the denominator silently shrinks to those who lasted, and since failure is the main reason funds close, the surviving set is systematically the lucky set. The same mechanism inflates reported returns for hedge funds, restaurant success stories ('most of our featured chefs are still open'), and back-tested trading strategies that quietly drop delisted stocks. The defense is a single question: what happened to the ones that are not in this average? If a rate's population was selected by an outcome related to the rate itself, the number is advertising, not measurement.

A screening test catches 90% of cases of a disease that affects 1% of people, and it wrongly flags 5% of healthy people. My friend tested positive and is terrified. Out of 10,000 people tested, how many positives are real?
Build the whole table; that is the only reliable way. Of 10,000 people, 1% have the disease:
100 cases. The test catches 90% of them, so 90 true positives. The healthy 9,900 get wrongly flagged at 5%:
495 false positives. Total positives: 90 + 495 = 585, of which the real ones are

15.4%. So a positive result, with a test that sounds excellent, still means roughly a 1-in-6.5 chance of actually having the disease, and a follow-up test is essential. The engine of the surprise is the base rate: because the disease is rare, the healthy pool is so vast that even a small false-positive rate manufactures far more positives than the disease does. Rates quoted for a test (sensitivity, false-positive rate) are computed within their own groups; the probability your friend cares about divides by all positives, a denominator that mixes both groups. Never let anyone quote you a test's accuracy without the base rate of the condition.
A retail chain announces 'December sales up 30%!' comparing December's $106,600 to November's $82,000. Last December was $102,500. Is the celebration justified?
Verify their comparison first:
+30.0%, arithmetically true. Now the comparison December deserves, against the same month last year, since retail is violently seasonal:

+4.0%. December always dwarfs November because of holiday shopping; comparing adjacent months in a seasonal business manufactures growth out of the calendar. The year-over-year figure, 4%, is the honest one, and it is decent but not a headline. The general defense: for any 'up X%' claim, ask 'compared with what?' The baseline is a choice, and it is usually chosen after looking at which choice gives the biggest number. Legitimate comparisons are fixed in advance: same period last year for seasonal data, the previous period for smooth data, and a stated average when a single period might be an outlier. A percentage change without a named baseline is a story looking for a number to wear.
Our support team boasts that the complaint rate fell from 3% to 2% this month. Complaints were 120 in both months. Orders rose from 4,000 to 6,000. Did anything actually improve?
Reproduce the boast. Month one:
3.0 complaints per 100 orders. Month two:

2.0. The rate genuinely fell by a third while the count did not move at all. Is that improvement? Partly, and it depends on what drives complaints. If complaints arise per order (a fixed chance each order goes wrong), then handling 50% more orders with the same failures really is better performance. If complaints arise per week (a broken help page generating a steady stream), then nothing improved and the falling rate is the denominator growing past a constant problem. The rate alone cannot tell you which world you are in; you need to know what the numerator is proportional to. Report both numbers always: the count (120, unchanged) and the rate (3.0% to 2.0%). A rate that improves only through its denominator deserves a footnote, not a bonus.

A retail chain picked its 8 worst stores by March defect rate, gave them a coaching program, and by April the group's average defect rate fell from about 9.7% to about 5.7%. The chain credits the coaching. Here are the stores' March and April rates in the data file. Should they?
Let me tabulate what actually happened, store by store:

arguments.code:
stores = [
    ("A", 14.4, 6.1), ("B", 11.8, 5.4), ("C", 10.5, 7.2), ("D", 9.6, 4.8),
    ("E", 8.9, 5.9), ("F", 8.1, 6.6), ("G", 7.4, 5.1), ("H", 6.9, 4.5),
]
mar = sum(s[1] for s in stores) / len(stores)
apr = sum(s[2] for s in stores) / len(stores)
print("March mean defect rate:", round(mar, 2))
print("April mean defect rate:", round(apr, 2))
print("Change in points:", round(apr - mar, 2))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
March mean defect rate: 9.7
April mean defect rate: 5.7
Change in points: -4.0

The fall is real: 9.7% to 5.7%, a drop of 4.0 points. The credit is the questionable part. These stores were selected because March was their worst month, and a store's monthly rate is its true defect level plus that month's luck: a broken batch, a flu week, a new hire. In April the luck re-rolled, average this time, so the rates drifted back toward each store's normal level even if coaching did nothing. This is regression to the mean, and it haunts every 'we intervened with the worst performers and they improved' story, from school turnarounds to CEO performance after a bad year. The honest test needs a comparison group: similar bad-March stores that got no coaching. If they fell by 3 points on their own, coaching added 1. Selecting on an extreme and watching it moderate is not evidence; it is arithmetic wearing a lanyard.
Two reports on the same country's jobs market, same week: one says unemployment is 4.2%, the other says 7.8%. The labor force is 164 million. One of them must be cooking the books.
Probably neither; they are likely using two official definitions with different numerators. The narrow measure counts people jobless, available, and actively searching: say 6.9 million of them.
4.2%. The broad measure adds discouraged workers who stopped searching and people working part-time involuntarily, a numerator of 12.8 million:

7.8%. Same week, same labor market, same denominator; the difference is entirely in who counts as unemployed. Neither is the 'real' rate in the abstract: the narrow one tracks active job search pressure, the broad one tracks total labor underuse, and each is the honest answer to its own question. Statistical agencies publish both precisely so no one has to choose blindly. The scandal version of this story, officials faking data, does happen in the world, but a two-definition gap is not evidence of it. When two rates disagree, compare the definitions before comparing the integrity of the people publishing them.

I want to build a simple price index for a weekly basket: 10 loaves of bread, 6 bottles of milk, 4 boxes of eggs. Last year they cost $2.00, $3.50, $4.00. This year $2.30, $3.85, $4.40. What is the index and what does it mean?
An index compares the cost of a fixed basket across time, with the base period set to 100. Cost the basket at last year's prices:
$57. The same basket at this year's prices:
$63.70. The index is the ratio scaled to 100:

111.8, meaning the basket costs 11.8% more than in the base year. Three disciplines make an index honest. The basket stays fixed, so the index measures prices, not shopping habits; if people switch from bread to rice, that is a different story. The quantities are the weights: eggs matter less than bread here because the basket holds fewer of them. And the base period must be named every time the index is quoted, because 111.8 is meaningless without 'last year = 100' attached. An index number is a rate in uniform: a ratio to a base, scaled for readability.
A price index stood at 100 in 2023, 108.4 in 2024, and 112.1 in 2025. A commentator says inflation is 'still over 12%'. Another says it fell to about 3.4%. Who is reading the index right?
The second one. An index level is cumulative; inflation is the change between periods. 2024's inflation:
8.4%. 2025's inflation is the change from 108.4 to 112.1, computed on the 2024 level:

3.41%. The first commentator subtracted the base (112.1 - 100 = 12.1) and called two years of accumulated increase a current rate. Prices are indeed 12.1% higher than in 2023, but the pace at which they are currently rising is 3.41% a year. Confusing a level with a rate of change is the index version of confusing a speedometer with an odometer. When you hear an inflation figure, ask: change between which two dates? An honest answer names both, and the denominator is always the earlier index value, never the base year, unless the claim is explicitly about the whole span.

Our old price index (base 2010 = 100) ended at 150 in 2020, when the agency rebased to 2020 = 100. The new series reads 118 in 2023. A client wants one continuous series on the old base. Can I just append 118 after 150?

Not directly: the two segments are ratios to different bases, so 118 on the new base is not smaller than 150 on the old. You splice by chaining through the overlap year, 2020, where both exist. On the new base, 2023 is 18% above 2020. Apply that same growth to the old series' 2020 value:
177. So on the old base, 2023 = 177, and the continuous series runs 100 (2010), 150 (2020), 177 (2023). The percentage change across the splice is preserved exactly:

18%, matching the new series' own change. Splicing works because an index only ever encodes ratios; rescaling a segment by a constant changes nothing about the changes inside it. The two ways to botch it are appending raw values (which fabricates a crash from 150 to 118) and re-basing the whole history by hand without the overlap (which invents data). Every long index series you have ever seen, including the famous consumer price indices, is a chain of such splices.
I got a 5% raise, from $60,000 to $63,000, but prices rose 7% this year. My manager calls it a raise. My wallet disagrees. Who is right in real terms?
Your wallet. Nominal change first, the one your manager quotes:
+5%. To get the real change, deflate the new salary by the price rise, expressing it in last year's purchasing power:
$58,878.50 in last year's dollars: less than the $60,000 you had. The real rate of change:

-1.87%. You took a real pay cut of about 1.9%. Note the method: real change is not 5 - 7 = -2, though that subtraction is a decent approximation at small rates; it is the ratio of the two growth factors, 1.05/1.07. The approximation and the exact answer drift apart as rates grow, which is why high-inflation economies wreck intuitions trained on subtraction. Any money series spanning years (wages, sales, house prices) should be deflated before anyone celebrates or mourns it. Nominal numbers measure currency; real numbers measure what the currency does.

A cost-of-living index weights rent at 40%, food at 30%, and transport at 30%. This year rent rose 10%, food 4%, transport 2%. What did the index do, and why is the answer not 5.33%, the plain average?
The plain average, (10 + 4 + 2)/3 = 5.33%, pretends the three categories matter equally. A weighted index lets each component pull in proportion to its share of spending:

5.8%. Rent's 10% rise contributes 4.0 points of that all by itself, because rent is 40% of the budget. Food contributes 1.2 points and transport 0.6. The general formula is the weighted mean: sum of (weight x change), with weights summing to 1. This is the same machinery as the mixture problem and the pooled rate: percentages must be averaged with their denominators' shares as weights, or the average lies. It also explains a common grievance: a household that spends 60% on rent experiences inflation of 0.6 x 10 + ... well above the published 5.8%, because its personal weights differ from the national basket. One index, many inflations; the official one belongs to the average basket, and nobody is the average.
In the same price index, luxury watches (weight 2%) jumped 50% in price, while housing (weight 25%) rose 4%. A headline screams about the watch prices. Which item actually moved the index more?
An item's effect on an index is its weight times its change, called its contribution. Watches:
1.0 index point. Housing:

Also 1.0 index point. The screaming 50% rise and the boring 4% rise moved the cost of living by exactly the same amount, because the boring item is twelve and a half times as large a share of spending. Contribution arithmetic is the antidote to headline inflation coverage: before reacting to any component's dramatic percentage, multiply by its weight. It is also how index statisticians explain their own releases ('energy contributed 0.3 of the 0.5 point rise'). A large percentage on a small weight is a rounding error with good public relations; a small percentage on housing, food, or energy is the index.
A factory's output index uses 2022 = 100. It made 1,200 units a month in 2022 and now makes 1,470. What is the production index, and how is it different from a price index?
Same construction, quantity instead of price. The index:
122.5, so output is up

22.5% on the base year. A price index holds quantities fixed and lets prices move; a quantity index like this one holds the comparison in physical units and lets volumes move. The two multiply into value: if this factory's prices also rose 10%, its revenue index would be roughly 1.225 x 1.10 = 1.3475, up about 34.75%. That decomposition (value = price x quantity) is one of the most useful habits in reading business news: when revenue jumps, ask how much was price and how much was volume, because a firm raising prices into shrinking volume is in a very different place from one selling more at steady prices. An index that does not say which it measures has told you only half its name.
An economics brief says our terms of trade improved because the export price index is 112 and the import price index is 105. What does that ratio mean in plain terms?
The terms of trade are a ratio of two indices: what you sell, priced against what you buy. Compute it:

106.7, up 6.7% from the base of 100. In plain terms: a given basket of exports now buys about 6.7% more imports than it did in the base year. If the numbers were reversed, the same exports would buy less. This is an index built from indices, a ratio of ratios, and it inherits the rules of both: it is only meaningful relative to its base period, and its change is a percentage change of a percentage-like quantity, so report it as 'improved 6.7% from base', never as '6.7 points of GDP' or anything grander. Ratios of indices appear everywhere once you look: real wages are a wage index over a price index, productivity is an output index over an hours index. Each is a comparison of two moving series compressed into one number that moves only when they diverge.
Our firm's sales were $8.0 million in 2022 and $9.6 million in 2026, up 20%. Over the same span the price level rose 18% (index 100 to 118). The board is celebrating 20% growth. Should they be?
Deflate the 2026 figure into 2022 dollars:
$8.136 million of real sales. Real growth over the four years:

1.69% total, not 20%. The nominal 20% decomposes into 18% of pure price and a sliver of volume. Put differently, if the firm had sold exactly the same physical volume at 2026 prices, sales would be $9.44 million; it actually beat that by only $160,000 over four years. None of this says the firm is failing: holding real volume while prices rise can be an achievement in a tough market. But a board steering by nominal growth in an inflationary period will systematically over-invest, over-hire, and over-borrow, because its dashboard confuses the currency's shrinkage with the firm's expansion. Deflate first, celebrate second.

An index rose 6% in year one and 6% in year two. A report says it stands at 112 (base 100). Then in year three it falls 6%, and the report says it is back to 106. How many errors are in that paragraph?
Two. First, chained changes multiply. After two years of +6%:
112.36, not 112. The report added 6 + 6 and skipped the compounding, the interest on the interest. Second, a fall of 6% from 112.36:

105.62, and more importantly it is not 'back' anywhere meaningful: +6% followed by -6% nets to 1.06 x 0.94 = 0.9964, an index of 99.64 against the start of that pair, a small loss, because the fall acted on the larger, risen base. The paragraph's errors are the two classics of this whole subject: adding percentages that should be multiplied, and assuming equal up and down percentages cancel. An index is a chained product of growth factors wearing a base of 100. Treat it as anything simpler and it will quietly misstate both booms and recoveries.

Daily case counts for the past week were 12, 15, 9, 14, 18, 11, 16. Our dashboard shows a 7-day average. Today brought 30 new cases. How does the average move, and why does the dashboard look calmer than the day feels?
The 7-day total:
95 cases, so the average is
13.57 a day. When today's 30 enters, the oldest day (12) leaves the window:

16.14. A day that more than doubled the typical count moved the headline number by only 2.57, because the new day is one seventh of the window and it also pushed out a below-average day. That smoothing is the point of a rolling average: it suppresses day-of-week noise and one-off reporting glitches. The cost is lag and blindness at turning points: the average describes the week that was, centered on its middle, so a genuine surge shows up as a gentle slope for days. Read the daily counts for detection and the rolling average for confirmation, and never let the calm of the average talk you out of what the raw days are shouting.
Our February sales were $280,000 and March sales were $310,000. The sales VP announced 10.7% growth. February had 28 days, March had 31. Is the announcement honest?
The arithmetic is:
+10.7%, exactly as announced. Now normalize by the length of the window. February per day:
$10,000 a day. March per day:

$10,000 a day. Identical. The entire 'growth' is three extra days of selling at an unchanged daily rate. Comparing totals over windows of different lengths is one of the oldest tricks in sales reporting, and February versus any month is its natural habitat, with 10% of phantom growth built into the calendar. The fix is mechanical: convert to a per-day rate before comparing, or compare against the same month last year. Whenever a growth claim spans two periods, check that the periods contain the same number of days, weekends, and holidays before you check anything else.
An ice cream brand's December sales were $20,000 against $95,000 in June, and a junior analyst flagged a 79% collapse. Last December was $18,000. What should the report actually say?
The analyst's number first:

-78.9%, June to December. But ice cream is seasonal: December is always a fraction of June, so the month-to-month change measures the calendar, not the business. The meaningful comparison is December against December:

+11.1% year over year. Same data, and the report flips from collapse to healthy growth. Year-over-year comparison is the standard vaccine against seasonality because it holds the season constant: whatever December does to ice cream, it did last December too. Its own weakness is that it is slow to reveal a fresh turn, since it averages a year of history into the baseline. Mature reporting shows both: year-over-year for the verdict on health, and a seasonally adjusted month-to-month for early warnings. What it never does is compare a peak month to a trough month and call the weather a crisis.

It is the 10th of the month and our sales are $96,000 month-to-date. Last month's full total was $310,000. My boss asks if we are 'way behind last month'. Last month's first 10 days were $88,000. What is the fair comparison?
Comparing 10 days against 31 is the mismatched-window error in its purest form. Compare like with like: the same first 10 days of last month:
You are 9.1% ahead of last month's pace, not behind. In daily-rate terms:

$9,600 a day against last month's $8,800 a day over the same stretch. If the pace simply held, the month would project to roughly 9,600 x 30 = $288,000 for a 30-day month, and the honest caveat is that pace rarely holds evenly: weekends, paydays, and month-end pushes bunch sales unevenly, so a projection from 10 days carries real uncertainty. The discipline for partial periods is to compare elapsed time against the same elapsed time in the reference period, and to label any full-period projection as a projection. 'Way behind' was an artifact of comparing a fraction to a whole.

Daily signups over nine days were 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 95, 85, 75, 65. Our growth lead keeps citing the rising 7-day rolling average as proof the trend is healthy. Run the numbers and tell me if she is right.
Here are the rolling averages, computed window by window:

arguments.code:
days = [60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 95, 85, 75, 65]
for i in range(len(days) - 6):
    window = days[i:i+7]
    print("days", i+1, "to", i+7, "rolling mean:", round(sum(window)/7, 2))
print("peak day:", max(days), "on day", days.index(max(days)) + 1)
print("last day vs peak:", round((days[-1] - max(days)) / max(days) * 100, 1), "percent")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
days 1 to 7 rolling mean: 82.86
days 2 to 8 rolling mean: 85.0
days 3 to 9 rolling mean: 84.29
peak day: 100 on day 5
last day vs peak: -35.0 percent

She is reading the average correctly and the situation wrongly. Signups peaked on day 5 at 100 and have fallen four straight days to 65, down 35% from the peak. Yet the rolling average rose from 82.86 to 85.00 before dipping only to 84.29, because a 7-day average is dominated by the strong days still inside its window and only sheds them one at a time. A rolling average is a trailing indicator by construction: its center of mass sits three to four days in the past. It is the right tool for confirming a trend and the wrong tool for spotting a turn. The turn is visible only in the raw series: four consecutive declines after a peak. Report both, and when they disagree, believe the raw data about what is happening now and the average about what was happening on average.
Our app loses 0.5% of its remaining subscribers every week. A teammate annualized that as 26% a year (0.5 x 52) and said we keep 74%. I suspect compounding changes it. Who is right?
You are. Weekly churn compounds on a shrinking base, exactly like interest in reverse. The fraction surviving 52 weeks:
77.0% survive, so the year's loss is

23.0%, not 26%. Your teammate multiplied the rate by the periods, which assumes each week loses 0.5% of the original base. In reality each week loses 0.5% of whoever is left, so the absolute losses shrink and the total lands lower. The gap between the naive 26% and the true 23% widens with the rate: at 2% weekly churn the naive figure says 104% gone, an impossibility, while compounding gives a survivable

35.0% remaining. Rule: a per-period percentage loss or gain is never annualized by multiplication. Raise (1 - rate) to the number of periods for survival, or (1 + rate) for growth, and let the exponent do the honesty.

Our quarterly revenues were 2.1, 2.3, 2.2, and 2.6 million. This quarter came in at 2.8. Why does our CFO quote a trailing-twelve-months figure of 9.9 million instead of just multiplying the new quarter by four?
Trailing twelve months (TTM) sums the last four actual quarters. Before this quarter:
9.2 million. The new quarter replaces the oldest one in the window:

9.9 million. Your CFO prefers it to annualizing the latest quarter (2.8 x 4 = 11.2 million) for two reasons. It uses only real results, no extrapolation; and it always contains exactly one of each quarter, so seasonal businesses are not flattered or damned by whichever quarter happens to be newest. The TTM growth rate is

7.6%. The trade-off is responsiveness: TTM changes by only the difference between the entering and leaving quarters, so it turns slowly, like the rolling average. It is a stability instrument. Use it for valuation and covenant tests; use the quarter itself, compared year over year, to detect what just changed.

Our factory had zero accidents last month, and the safety manager declared our accident rate is now zero. Over the trailing twelve months we had 11 accidents in 246,000 hours worked. Last month alone was 18,000 hours. How should we talk about this?
The trailing rate, per 100,000 hours:

4.47. That is your defensible accident rate: eleven events is enough mass to mean something. Last month's zero is a fact about one month, not a rate: with a true underlying rate of 4.47 per 100,000 hours, an 18,000-hour month expects about 0.8 accidents, so a zero month is the ordinary outcome, not a triumph. Watch the trap from the other side: had last month contained a single accident, its monthly rate would have been

5.56 per 100,000 hours, above the annual figure, and the same manager would be declaring a crisis. Short windows turn Poisson noise into headlines in both directions. The honest report: zero accidents last month, trailing-twelve-month rate 4.47 per 100,000 hours, trend judged on the long window. Safety, like rare disease, must be rated on exposure large enough to hold the events.
Driver A had 3 safety incidents in 2 weeks on the job. Driver B had 12 incidents in 50 weeks. The fleet manager wants to discipline B for having four times A's incidents. Fair?
Only if you ignore exposure, which is the entire story here. A's rate:
1.5 incidents per week. B's rate:
0.24 per week. A generates incidents at

6.25 times B's rate. By counts, B looks four times worse; by rates, A is more than six times riskier, and if both drove for 50 weeks at these rates, A would rack up roughly 75 incidents to B's 12. Counts over unequal windows or unequal exposure are not evidence; they are a measure of how long you watched. This is the same error as ranking hospitals by deaths without patient numbers. Two caveats keep the analysis honest: A's rate rests on only 2 weeks, so it is a shaky estimate that deserves monitoring rather than instant judgment; and incident severity is not in these numbers at all. But on the evidence as given, the manager's target is exactly backwards.

A dashboard averages our daily conversion rates: Monday 1 conversion from 10 visitors (10%), Tuesday 40 from 100 (40%), and it reports a 25% average conversion. Our actual orders and visitors say otherwise. Explain the bug.
The dashboard averaged the percentages: (10 + 40)/2 = 25%. But percentages from different-sized bases cannot be averaged unweighted. Pool the raw counts instead. Total conversions:
41. Total visitors:
110. The true conversion rate:

37.3%, not 25%. Tuesday carried ten times Monday's traffic, so the pooled rate rightly sits close to Tuesday's 40%. The dashboard's method gives a 10-visitor day the same vote as a 100-visitor day. This is the weighted-average rule again, the same one behind mixture concentrations and pooled clinical rates: to combine rates, add the numerators, add the denominators, and divide once at the end. Averaging finished percentages is only safe when every denominator is equal, which in real dashboards is almost never. If a tool offers you an 'average rate', ask whether it pooled the counts or averaged the percents; the wrong choice can be off by half, as it was here.
I drink a coffee with about 160 mg of caffeine at 8 in the morning. Caffeine's half-life in the body is roughly 5 hours. How much is left in me at 1 pm, 6 pm, and later?
A half-life means the amount halves every 5 hours, whatever the current amount is. At 1 pm, one half-life has passed:
80 mg. At 6 pm, two half-lives:
40 mg. After three half-lives, around 11 pm:

20 mg. After four, 10 mg. The sequence 160, 80, 40, 20, 10 shows the signature of exponential decay: equal time steps, equal proportions, shrinking absolute drops. It never formally reaches zero, which is why 'how long until it is gone' has no clean answer; the practical question is when it falls below the level that matters, here perhaps 10 mg by about 4 am. Half-life is the decline rate expressed in its most usable form: not a percent per hour, but the time per halving. Convert freely between them: a half-life of 5 hours corresponds to losing about 13% per hour, since 0.5^(1/5) is about 0.87.
Our club membership fell 50% during a bad year, from 2,000 to 1,000. This year we grew membership 50%. The president says we are whole again. We are not, are we?
