You are not, and by now the pattern should be familiar. The fall:
1,000 members. The 50% growth acts on 1,000:
1,500 members. You are still

25% below where you started. A 50% decline needs a 100% rise to repair it, because the rise is computed on the halved base. Declines deserve this extra care in reporting: a fall always sounds symmetric with the rise that 'matches' it, and the matching rise never matches. When the club reports the year, the honest sentence is: membership halved to 1,000, then recovered half of the loss to reach 1,500. Counts alongside percentages make the asymmetry impossible to hide, which is exactly why they should always travel together.

Our subscription service has 10,000 customers and loses 5% of them every month to churn. A colleague says we will lose 60% this year (5 times 12). What does the year actually look like if we add nobody?
Churn compounds on whoever remains, so survival after twelve months is 0.95 multiplied by itself twelve times:
54.0% of customers survive the year. The headcount:

5,404 customers, meaning the year costs you 46.0% of the base, not 60%. Your colleague multiplied a monthly rate by twelve, treating each month's loss as 5% of the original 10,000. In fact January loses 500, but December loses 5% of a much smaller base, about 285. This is the single most consequential compounding error in subscription businesses, because it runs the other way too: a deck that says 'only 5% monthly churn' is describing a business that must replace nearly half its customers every year just to stand still. Monthly rates always look tame. Annualize them by compounding before you judge them.

A reliability report on 600 devices shows failures by life stage: 18 failed in the first 3 months, 6 in months 4-6, and 24 in a later 3-month window in year three. The failure rate seems to fall then rise. Compute the hazards and explain the shape.
The hazard is failures divided by devices still alive at the start of each window. First window:
3.0%. Survivors entering the second window: 582. Its hazard:
1.03%. By year three, 576 devices remain, and the hazard climbs:

4.17%. High, low, high: this is the bathtub curve, the classic shape of failure over a product's life. Early failures are manufacturing defects and weak units dying young; the flat middle is the useful life, where failures are rare random accidents; the late rise is wear-out, parts genuinely aging. The managerial lesson is that 'the failure rate' of a product is not one number: quoting the 1.03% middle to a customer whose fleet is entering year three is a category error. Rates must be indexed to the age of the things being rated, which is why warranties, burn-in periods, and maintenance schedules are all shaped by this curve.
We bought a machine for $48,000. Accounting offers two depreciation stories: straight-line over 8 years, or declining balance at 25% a year. Compare the book values after three years.
Straight-line writes off the same amount each year:
$6,000 a year. After three years the book value is
$30,000. Declining balance writes off 25% of the current book value each year. After year one:
$36,000. After year two:
$27,000. After year three:

$20,250. So after three years, declining balance has written off $27,750 against straight-line's $18,000: it front-loads the expense, matching assets like computers that lose value fastest when young. Note the declining balance never reaches zero on its own (each year removes a quarter of what is left), which is why real schedules switch methods or set a floor. Depreciation is a rate story told two ways: constant absolute steps, or constant proportional steps. The asset does not care; the tax bill and the balance sheet do.
A radioactive sample starts with an activity of 800 becquerels and its half-life is 6 hours. What is the activity after 12 hours and after a full day?
Count half-lives, then halve that many times. Twelve hours is two half-lives:
200 Bq. A full day is 24 hours, four half-lives:
50 Bq. After two days, eight half-lives:

3.125 Bq. The practical power of the half-life form is that awkward times interpolate cleanly with the exponent: at 18 hours (three half-lives) it is 100 Bq, and at any time t the activity is 800 x 0.5^(t/6). Safety work leans on this: the rule of thumb that ten half-lives reduce activity to about a thousandth of the original (0.5^10 is 1/1024) lets a technician schedule when a space can be re-entered. Same mathematics as the caffeine in your bloodstream, different stakes: exponential decay is one pattern with many costumes.
A cup of coffee at 90 degrees sits in a 20-degree room. It loses about a quarter of the gap to room temperature every 10 minutes. What is its temperature after 10, 20, and 30 minutes?
The gap starts at 90 - 20 = 70 degrees. Losing a quarter of the gap each 10 minutes means keeping 75% of it. After 10 minutes the gap is 70 x 0.75 = 52.5, so the temperature is
72.5 degrees. After 20 minutes:
59.4 degrees. After 30 minutes:

49.5 degrees. This is Newton's law of cooling: the rate of cooling is proportional to the remaining gap, so the temperature decays exponentially toward the room's and never quite arrives. The practical reading: the coffee does most of its cooling early (17.5 degrees in the first 10 minutes, only 9.9 in the third), which is why a drink left 'for a minute' while you answer the door is already noticeably cooler, and why pre-warming the mug, which shrinks the effective early losses, works better than reheating later. Any process whose rate is proportional to what remains follows this curve: cooling, discharging capacitors, and drying paint.
A forest loses 2% of its area every year to clearing. A minister says at that rate half the loss over a decade is 20%, so 80% will remain. Check his arithmetic.
His instinct to multiply is the error we keep meeting. Each year removes 2% of what is standing, so the surviving fraction after ten years is 0.98 raised to the tenth power:

81.7% remains; the decade's loss is 18.3%, not 20%. The minister's linear estimate overstates the loss because it charges every year for 2% of the original forest, including trees already cleared. The gap is modest at 2% over ten years, but it grows with rate and horizon: at 10% a year, the linear guess says nothing remains after a decade, while compounding leaves

34.9% standing. None of this softens the policy problem: an 18.3% loss of a forest in ten years is severe, and the same exponential that cushions the arithmetic also means the clearing slows only because there is less left to clear. Report both the rate and the remaining stock; each disciplines the other.
We tracked 200 light bulbs. In month one, 30 failed. In month two, 8 of the survivors failed. In month three, 5 failed. Our supplier says the bulbs are 'getting more reliable every month'. Are they?
Compute the monthly hazard, failures over bulbs alive at the month's start. Month one:
15%. Month two, with 170 alive:
4.7%. Month three, with 162 alive:

3.1%. The hazard really is falling. But the bulbs are not improving; the population is changing. The weakest bulbs, the ones with manufacturing flaws, failed disproportionately in month one and left the pool. The survivors are a selected, hardier group, so their group failure rate drops even if no individual bulb changed at all. This is survivorship operating inside a rate over time, and it misleads constantly: rental cars 'become more reliable' with age, funds 'improve', patients on a treatment for years 'do better and better'. Some of that is real learning or maintenance; much of it is the frail leaving the denominator. Before crediting improvement, ask whether the group being rated is the same group that started.
A reservoir holds 1,000 units of water. Plan A caps usage so the stock drains 8% of whatever remains each week. Plan B rations a fixed 80 units a week. Compare the two after five weeks.
Plan A is exponential decay: each week keeps 92% of the previous stock. After five weeks:
659.08 units remain. Plan B is linear:

600 units. Plan A is ahead after five weeks, and the gap only widens, because its weekly draw shrinks with the stock (80, then 73.6, then 67.7 units...) while Plan B's never does. Run them to the end: Plan B empties the reservoir in exactly 12.5 weeks; Plan A never formally empties, passing 100 units only after about 27 weeks. The policy difference matters: a proportional rule is self-stabilizing but delivers ever less water, which users experience as tightening rationing; a fixed rule is predictable but hits a wall. Choosing between linear and exponential decline is choosing how the pain is distributed over time, and the arithmetic should be on the table when the choice is made.
Our library reading program enrolled 340 people, 290 attended at least one session, and 205 finished the program. The annual report needs a success rate. Which one do I print?
Print all three, labeled, because each is a real rate and they answer different questions. Finishers as a share of everyone enrolled:
60.3%. Finishers as a share of those who actually showed up:
70.7%. And the attendance rate itself:

85.3%. The 60.3% measures the program's reach-to-result pipeline and is the number a funder should see. The 70.7% measures how well the program serves people it actually touches. The 85.3% isolates the recruitment problem from the teaching problem: your program loses 15% before the first session and 29% of attenders along the way, two different leaks needing two different fixes. A single 'success rate' would have hidden which leak to repair. The honest rate report names its numerator, its denominator, and the question it answers; when in doubt, report the small table, not the single number.
A vaccine clinic gave 12,400 doses and saw 3 serious adverse events. A local post calls that 'a 3 in 12,400 risk, terrifying'. How should the clinic state the rate?
State it in the forms that let people judge it, with the counts attached. As a percentage:
0.024%. In the per-100,000 form used for rare events:

24.2 per 100,000 doses. Equivalently, about one event per 4,133 doses, since 12,400 divided by 3 is 4,133. Each framing is the same fact; the percentage is the least graspable at this smallness, which is why rare-event rates are quoted per 100,000 or as one-in-N. Two honesty requirements remain. First, the counts must travel with the rate, because 3 events is a small numerator: a single additional event would move the rate by a third, and readers deserve to know how fragile the estimate is. Second, a rate of harm means little without the rate of the harm prevented, the disease's own event rate in the unvaccinated, which is the comparison a decision actually needs. A rate quoted in isolation, however accurate, is half a report.

A treatment cuts the risk of a complication from 0.8% to 0.6%. The maker advertises a '25% risk reduction'. A critic calls it 'a measly 0.2% improvement'. Both cite the same trial. Who is misleading me?
Neither is lying; each picked the scale that serves them. The relative reduction:
25%, the maker's figure. The absolute reduction is 0.8 - 0.6 = 0.2 percentage points, the critic's. Now translate both into people. In 10,000 patients, the old risk produces
80 events; the new risk produces
60 events. Twenty events prevented per 10,000 treated, which means the number needed to treat for one person to benefit is

500. Now you can judge: a 25% relative cut sounds large, 0.2 points sounds trivial, and 'treat 500 people to spare one a complication' is the form a clinician can actually weigh against cost and side effects. The rule for reading any risk claim: demand both the relative and the absolute change, and the base rate underneath them. A relative change without its base rate is the single most abused statistic in health and finance alike.
A chart in a campaign leaflet shows approval rising from 41% to 44%, but the bars make it look like support quadrupled. The axis starts at 40. Quantify the trick for me.
The real change first. In points:
3 points. In relative terms:
A 7.3% increase in support. Now the chart's geometry. With the axis starting at 40, the visible bar heights are proportional to 41 - 40 = 1 and 44 - 40 = 4:

The second bar stands four times as tall as the first, visually claiming a quadrupling for a 3-point move. Bar charts encode value as length, and length must start at zero for the encoding to be honest; a truncated axis converts a modest change into a dramatic silhouette. (Line charts may truncate with more forgiveness, since they encode position and trend, but the axis break must be visible and labeled.) When a chart impresses you, read the axis before the shape. And when you make the chart, start bars at zero or choose a form that does not pretend length is value. The data said 'slight improvement'; the drawing said 'landslide'. Only one of them was the rate.

Our school's pass rate is 78% (156 of 200 students). The district average is 71% and the average for schools with similar intakes is 76%. Our head teacher quotes the 7-point gap. Is that the honest comparison?
Compute both gaps. Against the district:
7 points. Against similar-intake schools:

2 points. Both are true, and they support very different speeches. The district average pools wealthy and struggling schools alike; beating it by 7 points may say more about your intake than your teaching. The similar-intake comparison, the fair fight, says you are 2 points ahead of schools facing the same starting material: a real but modest edge. Choosing the comparison group is choosing the denominator of the argument, and it is often the most consequential choice in the whole report, made quietly before any arithmetic happens. The honest presentation gives both and explains why they differ. A useful habit: whenever a rate is praised or blamed, ask 'compared with whom, and who chose them?' If the answer is 'whoever makes the gap largest', you are reading advocacy, not analysis.
Our town of 21,500 had 860 emergency-room visits last year. The local paper wants a rate per 100 residents, and a state report wants per 100,000. Are these the same rate or two different statistics?
The same statistic at two magnifications. Per 100 residents:
4.0 visits per 100 residents. Per 100,000:

4,000 per 100,000. Neither is more correct; the base is chosen so the number lands in a range the audience can feel. A town paper quoting 4,000 per 100,000 forces readers to divide by a town that does not exist; a state report quoting 4.0 per 100 cannot distinguish towns whose rates are 4.02 and 4.04. The rule: pick the smallest standard base that gives a number with a whole part people can compare, and always print the base. Errors happen when the base is dropped in transmission: a 'rate of 4.0' clipped from the state table into the paper becomes nonsense. A rate without its base is like a price without its currency.

A trial of a rare side effect found 1 case in 50 patients, reported as a 2% rate. A second trial found 0 in 50, reported as 0%. The manufacturer says the risk has been eliminated. Comment on the arithmetic of small counts.
The rates are exact and nearly meaningless. One case in fifty:
2%. Zero in fifty: 0%. But look at the swing a single case commands. Had the first trial seen two cases:

4%: the rate doubles on one patient's outcome. Had the second trial seen one case, it would report the identical 2% as the first. With denominators this small, the difference between 0%, 2%, and 4% is one or two events, well inside what chance alone shuffles around. Statisticians handle this with uncertainty intervals, but the plain-language version serves most readers: with 0 events in 50 trials, rates up to roughly 6% are still consistent with the data (the old rule of three: 3/50). 'Eliminated' is a claim no 50-patient trial can carry. The honest report keeps the counts in front: 1 of 50, then 0 of 50, and lets the reader see how little evidence separates them.
A chocolate bar was 500 g at $5.00. Now it is 460 g at $5.60. The maker says the price rose 12%. A consumer group says the real rise is over 20%. Settle it with unit prices.
Both are describing a price; only one is describing the price of chocolate. The sticker change:
+12%, as the maker says. Now the unit price, per 100 g. Before:
$1.00 per 100 g. After, the bar holds 4.6 units of 100 g:
$1.2174 per 100 g. The unit-price rise:

21.7%. The consumer group is right about what a chocolate buyer actually pays: the 12% sticker rise and the 8% shrink multiply together (1.12 x 500/460 = 1.217). Shrinkflation works because the human eye tracks the price tag and the package size, rarely the ratio. The defense is the discipline from the cereal aisle: divide price by weight, every time, and compare the unit rates. A price is only meaningful per something; shrinkflation is what happens when the something quietly changes.
A jobs report headline says 'Pay up 4.1%'. Buried in the article, prices rose 5.3% over the same year. Write me the honest two-number summary of what happened to workers.
The nominal figure is 4.1%. The real figure deflates it by prices:

-1.14%. So the honest summary is two numbers, not one: pay rose 4.1% in currency, and fell 1.14% in purchasing power. The average worker's raise did not cover the year's price rises; each paycheck buys about 1.1% less than a year ago. Neither number alone suffices. The 4.1% matters for nominal things: a fixed-rate mortgage payment shrinks relative to pay, and tax brackets bite differently. The -1.14% matters for living standards. Reports that quote only the nominal figure in an inflationary year are technically accurate and functionally misleading, the same trick as the retailer comparing December to November. Train yourself to ask of every growth claim: nominal or real? If the answer is nominal and inflation is running, subtract roughly, or divide exactly, before reacting.

Audit this press release for me: 'Sales up 40%! Complaints down 50%! Customer satisfaction at a record 96%!' The underlying data: the 40% compares a $70,000 promo week to the worst week of the year, $50,000; the same week last year was $66,000, and the trailing four-week average is $63,500. Complaints fell from 8 to 4 a week, but weekly orders fell from 2,000 to 900. The 96% is 24 of 25 responses to a voluntary survey; the regular survey shows 88% from 2,000 responses. Write the corrected version.
Claim by claim. Sales: the release's baseline is the year's worst week. Against the same week last year:
+6.1%. Against the trailing four-week average:
+10.2%. A promo week beating both baselines is real, but it is 6 to 10%, not 40. Complaints: the count halved, but the rate is what matters. Before:
0.40% of orders. After:
0.44% of orders. Complaints per order actually rose; the count fell only because orders collapsed. Satisfaction: 24 of 25 is indeed

96%, from 25 self-selected responses; the standing survey of 2,000 customers says 88%, and voluntary surveys over-hear from the delighted and the furious. The corrected release: 'In our promotion week, sales were $70,000, up 6.1% on the same week last year and 10.2% above the recent four-week average. Orders fell to 900 in a quiet week; complaints numbered 4, a rate of 0.44% of orders, slightly above our usual 0.40%, which we are examining. Our regular customer survey (2,000 responses) puts satisfaction at 88%.' Every number survived; only the baselines, denominators, and sample sizes were restored. That is most of what auditing a rate claim ever involves.
